mcqs.question: Why does `Board.checkWinner(lastMove)` only inspect lines through the cell that was just played, instead of scanning the whole board?
options: Because only lines through the newest move could possibly have just become a winning line — every other line's state is unchanged from the previous check
Because scanning the whole board would produce incorrect results on boards larger than 3x3
Because Java cannot iterate over more than four lines efficiently
Because it lets the design skip storing the board state entirely
mcqs.explanation: A move can only complete a line that passes through the cell it was placed in — every other line is unaffected by this move, so checking them again is wasted work. Whole-board scans still give correct results on any size board; the optimization is about speed, not correctness. This has nothing to do with Java specifically, and the board state is still stored and read, just not re-scanned in full.

mcqs.question: What's the benefit of calling `WinChecker.generateLines(n)` once at game setup rather than recomputing the relevant lines on every move?
options: It moves the expensive combinatorial work (which grows fast with board dimension) to a one-time cost, leaving each move as a cheap lookup plus a small check
It is required because Java does not allow lists to be created inside a loop that runs more than once
It reduces the number of players the game can support
It removes the need for a `Board` class entirely
mcqs.explanation: Generating the line set once turns a potentially expensive, combinatorially-growing computation (especially visible in the 3D case) into a fixed setup cost — every move afterward is a cheap lookup. There's no such Java restriction, player count is unrelated, and `Board` is still needed to store cell state; `WinChecker` only owns the win-detection policy.

mcqs.question: Why does this design deliberately skip a State pattern for tracking whose turn it is?
options: State machines cannot be implemented in Java without external libraries
Turn order requires no other pattern because Strategy already handles it
Turn alternation is a single boolean/index flip with no guarded transitions or per-state behavior differences — the machinery a State pattern adds isn't earning its keep here
A State pattern would prevent bots from ever playing
mcqs.explanation: State pattern pays off when a mode change should trigger different behavior elsewhere (like Chess's check/checkmate flow) — plain turn alternation here is just flipping a value, so a full pattern is overkill. Java fully supports state machines; Strategy (for move selection) and turn-tracking are separate concerns; and none of this affects whether bots can play.

mcqs.question: In a networked version of this game, what actually fixes two clients submitting a move for the same turn at nearly the same time?
options: Locking the in-memory board object so only one thread can read or write it
Having each client wait a random delay before submitting a move
Storing two separate copies of the board, one per player
A server-side turn-sequence check that rejects any move whose expected turn number doesn't match the current turn
mcqs.explanation: The real risk is a stale or duplicate request claiming an already-resolved turn, not in-process thread contention — a turn-sequence check on the server rejects any move that doesn't match the current expected turn. A local lock doesn't address network-level staleness, random client delays are unreliable, and duplicating board state doesn't resolve which move is authoritative.

mcqs.question: Why must `Game.playTurn(move)` re-validate turn ownership and cell emptiness on the server, even if the UI already prevents invalid clicks?
options: Because client-side checks can be bypassed or raced (replayed requests, near-simultaneous taps, a non-UI client), so the server is the only place that can guarantee correctness
Because UI validation is always slower than server validation
Because the `Board` class cannot store more than nine moves without validation
Because Symbol enums require validation to be serialized correctly
mcqs.explanation: Any client-enforced rule can be bypassed by a different client, a replay, or a race condition — the server is the only trust boundary that can actually guarantee a move is legal before it changes state. This isn't about UI speed, board capacity, or enum serialization.
